polar-curves-s1.title: A polar rose, $r = 3\sin(2\theta)$, and its graph of $r$ against $\theta$
polar-curves-s1.text: The first graph shows $r = 3\sin(2\theta)$ as a function of $\theta$ on rectangular axes, for $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$. The second shows the same function drawn in the polar plane.

plot.label: Graph of r = 3 sin(2 theta) against theta for theta from 0 to 2 pi on rectangular axes, a wave between -3 and 3 with period pi

polar-curves-s2.title: The polar function $r = 1 + 2\cos\theta$
polar-curves-s2.text: The first graph shows $r = 1 + 2\cos\theta$ against $\theta$ on rectangular axes, for $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$. The second shows the same function in the polar plane.

plot.label: Graph of r = 1 + 2 cos theta against theta for theta from 0 to 2 pi, starting at 3, dipping to -1 at theta = pi, and returning to 3

items.q: How many petals does the polar curve $r = 3\sin(2\theta)$ have?

why.correct: For $r = a\sin(n\theta)$ with $n$ even, the rose has $2n$ petals: here $2\cdot 2 = 4$. On the $r$ against $\theta$ graph there are four humps on $[0, 2\pi]$, two above the axis and two below, and each hump draws one petal.
options: Each hump of the $r$ graph draws a petal, and there are four humps on $[0, 2\pi]$, including the two where $r < 0$.
That doubles the count twice. Four humps on $[0, 2\pi]$ draw four petals, each once.
An odd number of petals comes from an odd $n$; here $n = 2$.

items.q: For $\frac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \pi$, in which quadrant are the points of the curve drawn?

why.correct: On $\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)$ the $r$ graph is below the axis, so $r < 0$. The angle points into Quadrant II, and a negative $r$ sends each point backward through the pole, into Quadrant IV. That petal is the one centered on the ray $\frac{7\pi}{4}$.
options: Right: negative $r$ with an angle in Quadrant II lands in Quadrant IV.
That would need $r > 0$; the $r$ graph is negative on this interval.
The point opposite a Quadrant II direction is in Quadrant IV, not III.
Quadrant I points come from $0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}$, where $r > 0$.

items.q: What is the greatest distance from the pole to a point on the curve, and the first $\theta$ in $[0, 2\pi]$ where it occurs?

why.correct: The distance from the pole is $|r|$, largest when $|\sin(2\theta)| = 1$. First at $2\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$, so $\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$, where $r = 3$: the tip of the first petal.
options: Right: the first peak of the $r$ graph, the tip of a petal.
At $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$, $r = 3\sin\pi = 0$: the curve is at the pole.
The amplitude is $3$; the petal does not reach $6$.
$r = \frac{3}{2}$ at $\frac{\pi}{12}$ is partway out along the first petal.

items.q: For which $\theta$ in $[0, 2\pi)$ does the curve pass through the pole?

why.correct: The curve is at the pole where $r = 0$: $\sin(2\theta) = 0$, so $2\theta = 0, \pi, 2\pi, 3\pi$ and $\theta = 0, \frac{\pi}{2}, \pi, \frac{3\pi}{2}$. These are the zeros of the $r$ graph, where each petal begins and ends.
options: Right: the zeros of the $r$ graph.
Those are the tips of the petals, where $|r| = 3$.

items.q: Find the exact value of $r$ when $\theta = \frac{\pi}{12}$.

mistakes.why: That is $3\cos\frac{\pi}{6}$, or $3\sin\frac{\pi}{3}$ from doubling twice. $2\cdot\frac{\pi}{12} = \frac{\pi}{6}$, and $\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$.
Double the angle first: the input of sine is $2\theta = \frac{\pi}{6}$.

items.q: For which $\theta$ in $[0, 2\pi)$ does the curve $r = 1 + 2\cos\theta$ pass through the pole?

why.correct: $r = 0$ when $\cos\theta = -\frac{1}{2}$: $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\frac{4\pi}{3}$. On the $r$ graph these are where the curve crosses the $\theta$-axis.
options: At $\theta = \pi$, $r = -1$: the curve is $1$ unit from the pole.

items.q: Which interval of $\theta$ draws the small inner loop of $r = 1 + 2\cos\theta$?

why.correct: The inner loop is traced while $r < 0$, between the two zeros: on $\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}, \frac{4\pi}{3}\right)$ the $r$ graph is below the axis. The angles point left, but negative $r$ puts the points to the right of the pole, inside the big loop.
options: Right: the interval where $r$ is negative.
$r = 1$ at $\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\frac{3\pi}{2}$; $r$ is still positive at the ends of this interval.
There $r > 0$: that piece is the upper half of the big loop.
There $r > 0$: that piece is the lower half of the big loop.

items.q: What are the rectangular coordinates of the point on $r = 1 + 2\cos\theta$ where $\theta = \pi$?

why.correct: $r = 1 + 2\cos\pi = -1$. Then $x = r\cos\theta = (-1)(-1) = 1$ and $y = r\sin\theta = 0$. The angle points left, and the negative $r$ sends the point $1$ unit to the right: the far end of the inner loop.
options: Right: $r = -1$ at angle $\pi$ is the point $(1, 0)$.
That treats $r = -1$ as a distance in the direction $\pi$; a negative $r$ reverses the direction.
The angle $\pi$ is on the horizontal axis, so $y = 0$.

items.q: Which point of $r = 1 + 2\cos\theta$ is farthest from the pole?

why.correct: The distance from the pole is $|r|$. On the $r$ graph, $|r|$ is largest at $\theta = 0$ (and $2\pi$), where $r = 3$. That point is $(3\cos 0, 3\sin 0) = (3, 0)$.
options: Right: $|r| = 3$ is the largest value of $|r|$.
At $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$, $|r| = 1$; that point is $1$ unit away.
$r = 3$ happens at $\theta = 0$, which points right, not up.
A circle of diameter $4$ centered at $(2, 0)$
A circle of radius $4$ centered at the pole
A circle of diameter $4$ centered at $(0, 2)$

why.correct: Multiply by $r$: $r^2 = 4r\cos\theta$, so $x^2 + y^2 = 4x$. Complete the square: $(x - 2)^2 + y^2 = 4$, a circle of radius $2$ (diameter $4$) centered at $(2, 0)$. It passes through the pole at $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$.
options: That is $r = 4$, with $r$ constant; here $r$ changes with $\theta$.
A sine, $r = 4\sin\theta$, gives the circle centered on the vertical axis.
A circle of radius $5$ centered at the pole

why.correct: $r = 5$ for every $\theta$: every point is $5$ units from the pole, in every direction. That is the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 25$.
options: A fixed angle gives a line through the pole; this fixes the distance.

items.q: Which polar equations have a cardioid as their graph? Select every one.

why.correct: A cardioid is a limaçon $r = a + b\cos\theta$ or $r = a + b\sin\theta$ with $|a| = |b|$: the curve just touches the pole once.
options: Not a cardioid: $|a| < |b|$, so the limaçon has an inner loop.
Not a cardioid: a rose with $3$ petals.
Not a cardioid: $|a| > |b|$, so the limaçon never reaches the pole.

items.q: How many petals does the rose $r = 2\cos(3\theta)$ have?

why.correct: For $r = a\cos(n\theta)$ with $n$ odd, the rose has $n$ petals. Here $n = 3$. Over $[0, 2\pi]$ the curve traces the three petals twice, because the negative-$r$ humps redraw them.
options: $2n$ petals is the rule for even $n$; for odd $n$ the negative humps land on the same petals.
$2$ is the length of each petal, not the count.
That is $n^2$; the count is $n$ for odd $n$.

items.q: For the limaçon $r = a + 2\cos\theta$, the value of $a$ increases from $2$ to $4$. Predict how each feature changes.

variables.name: The greatest distance from the pole
variables.why: The greatest distance is $a + 2$, at $\theta = 0$, so it goes from $4$ to $6$.

variables.name: The angle θ at which the greatest distance occurs
variables.why: $a + 2\cos\theta$ is largest where $\cos\theta = 1$, at $\theta = 0$, whatever the value of $a$.

variables.name: The least distance from the pole
variables.why: The least value of $r$ is $a - 2$, at $\theta = \pi$: it goes from $0$ (a cardioid touching the pole) to $2$.

why.correct: Raising $a$ adds the same amount to every $r$: the curve grows outward and pulls away from the pole, while its widest point stays on the polar axis.

items.q: Put the steps for sketching a polar curve from its graph of $r$ against $\theta$ in order.
options: Read $r$ at $\theta = 0$, $\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\pi$ and $\frac{3\pi}{2}$, and mark the zeros of $r$
Note where $r$ is positive and where it is negative
Plot each point: turn to $\theta$, move $|r|$ units, backward through the pole when $r < 0$
Join the points in order of increasing $\theta$

why.correct: Key values first, then signs, then plotting with the sign rule, then joining in the order the angle sweeps.

items.q: Which describes the graph of $r = \theta$ for $0 \le \theta \le 4\pi$?
options: A spiral that winds outward, two full turns
A ray from the pole at angle $4\pi$

why.correct: As $\theta$ sweeps around, $r$ keeps growing: each point is farther from the pole than the last, so the curve winds outward. From $0$ to $4\pi$ the angle makes two full turns.
options: Right: growing distance with a turning angle makes a spiral.
A circle needs $r$ constant; here $r$ grows with $\theta$.
A ray needs $\theta$ constant; here $\theta$ changes.
A rose needs $r$ to rise and fall back to $0$; here $r$ only grows.
